libadb-android 3.1.1, local maintenance patch 2026-10-03

Upstream: https://github.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android
Tag: 3.1.1
Tag archive SHA-256:
8cdb9b909991ab96da211b293175357345c9d727a22221f36b8d573da7bb1de8

The library's Apache-2.0 alternative is selected, together with the retained
BSD-3-Clause and MIT terms in individual source headers. See COPYING, LICENSES,
and upstream-manifest.json for the unmodified import's file digests.

Local changes:
- AdbConnection.open waits on acknowledged/closed state, not an unconditional
  notification. This prevents early OKAY/CLSE loss and spurious-wake success.
  An acknowledged command that has already finished is distinct from an OPEN
  rejected without acknowledgement, including commands with empty output.
- Failed/interrupted opens unregister and close their unreturned stream.
  Late acknowledgements receive a matching CLSE instead of leaking a peer channel.
- Stream ID allocation is synchronized; acknowledgement wakes all state waiters.
- AbsAdbConnectionManager snapshots the connection under its lock and opens the
  stream outside it, so a pending OPEN cannot block physical disconnect.
- AdbStream exposes an internal acknowledgement-state check.
- A peer close with unread output drains all queued/buffered bytes and then
  reaches EOF instead of waiting forever. Writers reject that known peer close
  even while the reader still owns buffered output.
- Abrupt transport loss is not reported using the clean peer-EOF exception, so
  partial shell/catalog output cannot masquerade as a successfully completed read.
  AdbInputStream delegates closure to that distinction, drains already buffered
  bytes, returns unsigned single-byte values and accepts zero-length reads without
  waiting for remote data.
- v2.4.2: Every outgoing WRTE fragment waits for its own OKAY. Empty and invalid
  writes do not consume write credit, and concurrent logical writes are serialized
  with interruptible cancellation.
- Incoming payload acknowledgement moves to the consumer. One queued packet may
  wait beside the current read buffer; another uncredited queued packet fails the
  transport explicitly rather than growing memory without bound. Other channels
  remain independent. Empty WRTE packets are acknowledged without becoming EOF.
- Local close immediately unregisters its channel and refuses late input. Read
  availability retains buffered peer output and distinguishes transport failure
  from a received clean peer close.
- v2.5.0: Abrupt stream transport loss uses AdbTransportException so callers can
  recover without string-matching or treating a truncated read as clean EOF.
  Connection failure retains its original cause for timeout/TLS diagnostics.
- v2.5.1: A writer, flush or packet read that reaches an ended transport reports
  AdbTransportException, and one received CLSE is reported identically to a
  channel's reader and writer, so recovery no longer depends on which thread
  noticed the loss first. Using a connection after its reader thread stopped
  reports transport loss instead of IllegalStateException. The TCP connect is
  bounded by the manager's existing connection timeout, so an address that never
  answers cannot hold the manager lock for the kernel's SYN timeout.
- v2.6.0: An OPEN packet is sized from the destination's UTF-8 bytes rather than
  its UTF-16 length, so a service name with non-ASCII text (for example a camera
  named in the device's language) no longer overflows the packet buffer.
- v2.15.0: A stream keeps output the peer sends before it was acknowledged, up to
  2 MiB per stream, instead of failing the whole connection on a second queued
  packet. Android 16's adbd sends a shell command's last output early as the command
  ends, which ended the mirroring session on the next read. A peer that ignores
  acknowledgement altogether still fails the transport once that bound is passed.
  app/src/test/.../adb/AdbFlowControlTest.kt drives a small adbd through such output
  and past the bound, and AdbStreamOpenTest's queue-bound case now fills 2 MiB first.
- v2.16.0: Wireless-debugging pairing uses Spake2.java, a Java port of BoringSSL's
  SPAKE2 (spake25519.cc, Apache-2.0, Copyright 2016 The BoringSSL Authors), instead
  of the spake2-android 2.2.1 library, which was LGPL-3.0 with a native libspake2.so.
  Field arithmetic is Bouncy Castle's constant-time X25519Field, and every scalar
  multiplication is a Montgomery ladder over all 256 bits with the complete Edwards
  addition law. PairingAuthCtx.java uses it; libadb's build no longer depends on
  spake2-android. Tests: src/test/java/.../Spake2Test.java (RFC 8032 keys, BoringSSL's
  M and N, agreement, peers without the 2017 password-scalar fix, corrupted messages);
  the app's androidTest Spake2InteropTest checks it against the old native library,
  kept as a test-only dependency; WirelessDebuggingLiveTest pairs with a real adbd.
- v2.16.0: TLS no longer accepts any certificate. AdbTrustManager.java accepts what
  adbd always presents, one self-signed certificate for an RSA (2048 bits or more) or
  EC (256 bits or more) key, and refuses anything else, such as a chain an intercepting
  proxy's authority issued. adbd's certificate is for a key it creates when it starts,
  so it cannot be pinned, and AOSP's adb host accepts any server certificate; pairing
  is authenticated by SPAKE2 over TLS-exported keying material, and the device admits
  only paired keys. SslUtils.java uses it for pairing and for connecting.

- v3.5.6: The peer's CNXN max-data is clamped to the host's own maximum for the API
  level (as AOSP's host does) and a value <= 0 fails the connection as a protocol error,
  so a hostile adbd can no longer force ~2 GiB per-stream/packet allocations or make
  AdbStream.write spin on empty WRTEs (which also refuses a non-positive chunk size).
  Test: app/src/test/.../adb/AdbHostileMaxDataTest.kt.
- v3.5.6: PairingConnectionCtx bounds the TCP connect (10 s) and the TLS handshake and
  every pairing read (15 s socket timeout), keeps its raw and TLS sockets in fields,
  closes them when the TLS setup fails and in close(), and close() tolerates a context
  that never got as far as creating streams or the PAKE state. (No JVM test: it needs a TLS/Conscrypt peer.)

Modified files, each marked with a notice under its license header:
AbsAdbConnectionManager.java, AdbConnection.java, AdbInputStream.java,
AdbProtocol.java, AdbStream.java, PairingAuthCtx.java, PairingConnectionCtx.java,
SslUtils.java and android/AdbMdns.java.
AdbTransportException.java, AdbTrustManager.java and Spake2.java are new.

The Android build uses the app's existing SDK, Bouncy Castle and toolchain.
Pairing and authentication, the wire protocol and its cryptography follow upstream
and AOSP; SPAKE2 is the Java port described above. The old binary artifact is replaced, not packaged alongside
this module. The existing app deadline and failure paths are retained.

Regression evidence: app/src/androidTest/.../adb/AdbStreamOpenTest.kt runs a
loopback protocol peer with early replies, spurious wakes, timeout/cancellation,
late acknowledgements, concurrent opens and physical disconnect. Reflection
used to control scheduling exists only in the debug instrumentation fixture.
Additional cases cover packet-by-packet write credit, bounded per-channel receive
backpressure, empty packets, invalid writes and cancellation without peer replies,
writers and opens after transport loss, a handshake the peer closes, a connect
that is never answered, and a non-ASCII OPEN destination. TlsTransportFailureTest
checks how the bundled Conscrypt provider reports a reset after the TLS handshake.
- v3.1.1: Once the peer refuses the signature and receives the public key (the
  device is showing "Allow debugging?"), connect() waits an optional, bounded
  extra time (setUserAuthorisationTimeout) and reports the moment through
  setUserAuthorisationListener. Without it a first connection failed after the
  10-second network timeout while the user was still reaching for the device.
- v3.4.0: SslUtils, AbsAdbConnectionManager, AdbConnection and AdbMdns no longer use
  System.out.println/printStackTrace; they log through android.util.Log.w (no stdout/stderr leakage).
